title: Rules for discernment
hookLine: learning to read the movements of the heart

lines: A SOLDIER IN BED, WITH THE WRONG BOOKS.
cards: A wounded soldier is stuck in bed, bored, in a house with the wrong books: no adventure stories, only a life of Christ and lives of the saints. So he alternates.
For hours he daydreams about a great lady and glorious deeds. Then he reads, and daydreams about doing what the saints did. Both daydreams are pleasant while they last.
But afterward, as Ignatius tells it later, he notices something odd. The knightly dreams leave him dry and unsatisfied. The saintly ones leave him content, long after the book is closed.
He starts paying attention to the aftertaste.

teach.b: Back on day two hundred thirty-eight you met consolation and desolation; here are the rules behind them. In everyday speech, discernment means sound judgment. Ignatius means something narrower.
His Rules for the Discernment of Spirits are about the movements inside a person: the pulls, moods and thoughts that come and go.

Consolation is any movement that draws a person toward God: more faith, hope and love, a quiet peace, even tears. Desolation is the reverse: darkness, restlessness, a drag toward low things, feeling far from God.

The subtle part: the same feeling can mean opposite things, depending on which way a person is heading. For someone drifting away from God, the enemy offers easy pleasures, and the good spirit stings the conscience.
For someone growing toward God, it flips: the enemy stings and discourages, and the good spirit gives courage and peace. So a feeling isn't a verdict. It's a signal, read in context.
The First Letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits if they be of God."
One plain rule: in a time of desolation, make no change. Stay with what you decided in a clearer hour. And in consolation, store up strength for the next dark stretch.

teach.h: TELL IT TO A WISE GUIDE.
teach.b: The enemy, he adds, wants secrets kept, and loses power once things are told to a wise confessor or guide.

teach.h: TRY THE SPIRITS IF THEY BE OF GOD.
teach.b: And if a dark stretch ever turns into not wanting to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

how: People who pray in the Ignatian way use the rules for discernment of spirits throughout a retreat and in daily life, often talking over their consolations and desolations with a spiritual director.

o: having good taste in art, food or music
a gift for seeing the future in dreams
learning to read the heart's pulls toward God

games.q: reading the heart — tap the pairs.
p: a movement toward God: peace, hope, love
test whether they be of God

s: for Ignatius, a good feeling always means God and a bad one the enemy
it depends which way a person is heading. the good spirit can sting, and the enemy can soothe.
Ignatius says not to make a change in a time of desolation
stay with what you decided in a clearer hour.
Ignatius first noticed these movements while recovering from a wound
reading the saints, he noticed which daydreams left him dry and which left him content.

games.q: you're in a dark, restless stretch, and you want to drop a commitment you made in a peaceful time. what do Ignatius's rules say?
o: drop it now, while you feel it so clearly.
hold steady: make no change in desolation.
make some other big decision to feel better.
games.why: in desolation, make no change; stay firm in what you decided before. the dark stretch is the wrong time to redraw the map.

practice: Let today replay quickly, like flipping through photos on a phone, and stop at one moment that left a good aftertaste, then at one that left you dry or restless.
Just name them, this drew me toward, this pulled me away, without analyzing. If you pray, bring both to God and ask for light to read them.

wordCard.voice: Discernment. For Ignatius, learning to read the movements of the heart, consolation and desolation, and where each one leads. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a sorting, a telling apart. Paul names the discerning of spirits among the gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:10.

carryVoice: Your line: read the heart. It began with a soldier noticing an aftertaste. I'll be here tomorrow.
